title: You say start early but also wait. Which is right for a fresh graduate?
excerpt: A fresh graduate points out that Sean tells young people both to start early and to build a safety net first. Sean explains it depends on your career, risk appetite and goals.

question.context: A fresh graduate wrote in about advice that seems to contradict itself: start accumulating property early to make use of the 35-year loan, yet earn at least RM5,000 and build a safety net first. Meanwhile prices keep rising faster than salaries, and he fears young people will be priced out.
question.text: What mindset should fresh graduates and first-time buyers have about when to start in property?

answer.quote: Property investment is only a way of wealth building.
answer.summary: It depends on who you are. If you are on a stable salaried career path, buying an investment property early makes sense. If you want to get rich, or are building a business or side project, invest in yourself and the business first, and put money into property once you have earned it.

reasons.title: Property suits people with certain income
reasons.body: Sean bought early because he planned to climb the corporate ladder, with a salary arriving every month. Over about ten years the rent and value rose, and he refinanced to take out the equity his tenants built.

reasons.title: Property is too slow to make you rich
reasons.body: Quick flips are largely over. A RM400,000 unit may rise only about 15% in ten years, far slower than young people expect.

reasons.title: A loan takes away flexibility
reasons.body: You need an emergency fund and money for repairs and empty months, and you can no longer quit a job or join a friend's venture freely. That is a real cost while your career is still taking shape.

reasons.title: Never has building a business been cheaper
reasons.body: Online shops, social media and free tutorials make starting a business far easier than before. Commission-based work, like property or insurance agency, rewards effort directly; invest the earnings afterwards.

actions: Decide whether your path is a stable salaried career, commission work, or a business.
If salaried and certain, consider an investment property early, even renting a room yourself while it is let out.
If you are building something on the side, put your money into that first.
Don't overspend on a first own-stay home just to own a landed house.
Compare property with other options, such as ETFs, index funds and stocks, before committing.
caveat: Fear of being priced out often reflects doubt about your own future income. If you are willing to work hard and invest in yourself, waiting a few years is rarely the end of the world.
sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #195. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as Sean stated them in December 2022.
